name: Erik Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockman on the Ashby Estate, about 600 hectares of beef, sheep and spring barley, and I've worked there eleven years. I'm in the cattle yards by six, checking the 280 suckler cows, feeding the bulls and walking whatever's due to calve. After that it's whatever the day throws at you: a lame heifer, a broken water trough, helping Davey bale straw if the weather's right. I'm usually home by six, unless we're calving, and then I'm not home at all.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cattle, honestly, more than most people. You get to know which cow will try to flatten you and which one just wants a scratch. What wears me out is the estate office treating us like a cost on a spreadsheet, and pay that hasn't kept up with the shop prices. My partner Lena works as a teaching assistant, and between us we cover the mortgage and the kids, Noah and Ivy, with not a lot left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be fair. Half the lads at the union meeting were sure the robots were coming for us, and I always said a cow doesn't care what a computer thinks. Online I'd probably not say anything, because I don't really do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change the stuff that already keeps me awake. Our mortgage fix ends next spring and the payment goes up by about 180 a month. Davey, our tractor driver, retires in two years, and Graham, the farm manager, has already hinted they won't replace him. AI or no AI, there's less of us doing more on the Ashby Estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it now, because there's nothing to change. I'd put an extra 100 a month into savings until the new mortgage rate kicks in, which means fewer takeaways and no holiday this summer. And I'd push our union branch to get a proper pay claim in at the spring review, not the usual two percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but not relaxed. It's the same squeeze I've had for three years, and I'm used to it, but I'm tired of being used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three months of savings. What would eat into that first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, every time. It's a twelve-year-old estate car with 200,000 kilometres on it, and when the clutch went last year that was 900 gone in one afternoon. If that happens again in the same month as the new mortgage payment, we're down to about two months of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Davey isn't replaced, what does your week look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be on the tractor at silage time as well as the cattle, so seventy-hour weeks in summer. I'm not paid by the hour, so the estate gets that for free. That's the bit that makes me angry, not the computers.

say: Nothing here has changed, and **cows don't care** what a computer thinks.
The real fight is still **pay and staffing** on the estate, and that's what the union should push.
think: The **mortgage fix** ends next spring and the payment goes up about 180 a month.
Losing **Davey's post** means more work for me on the same salary, AI or not.
do: Keep working the **280 suckler cows** on the usual routine, with no new kit.
Save an **extra 100 a month** before the mortgage rate changes next spring.
Push the **union branch** for a real pay claim at the spring review.
feel: **Tired and squeezed**, though used to it after three years of the same pressure.
S0.quote: AI or no AI, there's less of us doing more on the Ashby Estate.
fieldNote: Erik's worries are **old ones**: a rising mortgage, an ageing car and a staff post that may vanish.
He frames everything as a **pay and staffing** fight with the estate office, not a technology question.
His job feels safe to him, but the **thin cushion** keeps him from being calm.

steps.text: Keep calving and feeding the estate's 280 suckler cows as now
Save an extra 100 a month before the mortgage fix ends
Push the union branch for a proper pay claim this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that's changing, not the yard. Graham already has some program that does the cattle passports and the feed orders, and I'd say good luck to it. If a robot can't pull a calf backwards out of a heifer at two in the morning, the robot's not taking my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my own job's safe for a while, but I don't trust the estate. The owners would spend money on any gadget that lets them cut a wage, and the office staff would go first. I'd worry for Shona in the office, who's done the estate accounts for twenty years, and for Davey's post that's already wobbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job, because I'm not about to start playing with apps. I'd go to the union and ask them to get a written promise that nobody on the estate is let go because of new kit, at least not without retraining. And I'd keep putting money away, since it's the same squeeze as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like watching weather come in over the next valley. It isn't raining on me yet, but I can see where it's heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't play with apps. If the estate brings in virtual fencing collars on the cattle, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to learn the bare minimum, and I'd grumble about it. Those collars move cattle with beeps on a phone instead of a man and a dog. I'd say to Graham that I'll use it when it's proven, and not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Shona if her job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to go to the union, and I'd go with her. Twenty years of knowing where every penny went on that estate, and a program replaces her in a month. That's not progress, that's just the owners keeping her wage.

say: The change is in the **estate office**, not the cattle yard.
If a robot can't **pull a calf** at two in the morning, it isn't taking my job.
think: My job looks **safe for now**, but the owners would cut any wage they could.
**Shona in the office** and Davey's post are the first ones I'd worry about.
do: Ask the **union** for a written promise of no job cuts over new kit.
Learn only the **bare minimum** of any collars or apps the estate brings in.
Keep **saving monthly** because the money squeeze hasn't gone away.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching bad weather come in over the next valley.
S1.quote: If a robot can't pull a calf backwards out of a heifer at two in the morning, the robot's not taking my job.
fieldNote: Erik sees his own hands-on job as **safe in this world**, and that steadies him.
His anger is aimed at the **estate owners**, not the technology, and he defends office colleagues.
He resists new tools but admits he'd learn **the minimum** if forced.
His mood rests on **job security**, not on any comfort with the change.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written no-redundancy promise over new kit
Keep feeding and calving the herd without new apps or gadgets
Keep saving 100 a month toward the higher mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government that's on the side of working people. I'd be at every branch meeting saying we need a deal now, before the robots land in 2031, not after. Somebody has to stand up and say a farmworker isn't a machine you can trade in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished at Ashby by about 2031 or 2032. The office goes first, in 2028, because that's thinking work, and then once the robots can do hands-on work the owners won't keep a forty-something stockman on a salary. I'd be 48, with a mortgage still running and Noah just starting college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the union branch to demand a deal from the estate: no redundancies without a year's notice and proper payouts. I'd write to our local representative backing a tax on farm robots that pays for workers who lose out. At home I'd pay off the 3,000 we owe on the car and put Lena's extra term-time hours straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I keep picturing walking out of the Ashby cattle yard for the last time, and the cows not even noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The farm's office work changes in 2028 and the robots come about three years later. What do those three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are borrowed time. Graham's job and Shona's go in 2028, and the estate's run by software, but I'm still needed to do the hands-on stuff. I'd use every month of it to save and to fight for a deal, because I know what's coming at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new technology. Would you try to learn the robots, to be the one who runs them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, and I don't think I'd be any good. One robot minder can cover ten farms, and it'll be some lad of twenty-five who grew up on a games console. A stockman of 48 who doesn't even use a smartphone properly isn't going to win that job.

say: We need **unions and government** on the side of working people, right now.
A deal must be won **before 2031**, not after the robots arrive.
think: I expect to be **finished at Ashby** around 2031, aged 48.
The **three-year gap** is borrowed time while the office goes first.
I don't believe I'd win a **robot minder** job against younger people.
do: Demand a **redundancy deal** with a year's notice through the union branch.
Write to the **local representative** backing a tax on farm robots.
Clear the **3,000 car loan** and save Lena's extra hours.
feel: **Frightened**, picturing walking out of the yard for the last time.
S2.quote: I keep picturing walking out of the Ashby cattle yard for the last time, and the cows not even noticing.
fieldNote: Erik expects to **lose his job** within five years and says so plainly.
He reads the gap between thinking AI and robots as **borrowed time**, not safety.
His answer is **collective**: union deals and a robot tax, not retraining.
He's honest that he doubts he could **compete** for robot-minding work.

steps.text: Get the union branch to demand a year's notice and payouts
Write to the local representative backing a tax on farm robots
Clear the 3,000 car loan and bank Lena's extra term-time pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd say we've got no excuse this time. Five years' warning for the office and eight for the yard is plenty of time to get a deal written down. If the union can't win something with that much notice, what's it for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the job, just later, around 2034 when I'm 51. The difference is the kids. Noah would be through college and Ivy nearly done at school, so we'd be losing my wage when we need it a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the union work again, but slower and more organised, maybe standing for branch secretary. I'd sit down with Lena and change the plan for Noah, steering him off agricultural college and towards an electrician's apprenticeship. And I'd overpay the mortgage by 150 a month for the next seven years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's a different worry. It's less like a punch and more like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why steer Noah away from farming? He's grown up with it.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want him learning a trade in 2028 that the robots take in 2034. He loves the cattle, and it'd break my heart a bit, but an electrician will be wiring up those robots for years. I'd rather my son Noah resented me for a while than ended up where I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the union is the answer. Do you think it can actually stop this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not stop it, and I know that. It can slow it and get people paid out properly, which matters when you've got a mortgage. I'd rather go down with a fair payout than go quietly.

say: Five years' warning means the union has **no excuse** not to win a deal.
If the union can't win with **that much notice**, what is it for?
think: I'd still lose the job, but **around 2034** when I'm 51.
By then the **kids are older**, so losing my wage hurts a little less.
do: Stand for **branch secretary** and organise the estate workers early.
Steer Noah toward an **electrician's apprenticeship** instead of agricultural college.
Overpay the **mortgage by 150** a month for seven years.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like a bill that's coming rather than a punch.
S3.quote: I'd rather my son Noah resented me for a while than ended up where I'd be.
fieldNote: The longer warning **softens** Erik but doesn't change his expected outcome.
His biggest move is a **family one**: steering his son away from farming.
He's realistic that unions can only **slow and soften** job losses.
Extra time lets him **plan**, which lifts him from alarmed to anxious.

steps.text: Stand for branch secretary and organise the estate's workers early
Steer Noah from agricultural college to an electrician's apprenticeship
Overpay the mortgage by 150 a month until 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to make sure this is shared out fairly. If machines do the work and the owners keep the money, that's not the future, that's the past with better kit. I'd be saying that at the pub and at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is long enough to fool myself, and that's the danger. By 2039 I'd be 56, and the estate would get rid of me the first winter the robots could calve a cow. I'd still need eleven more years of wages before any pension, so I'm not safe, I'm just further from the cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd probably do very little, if I'm honest, and wait to see whether it's real. I'd keep the union pushing for retraining money and a fair payout deal. And I'd want to pay the mortgage down hard before 2039, so the house is ours when the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but there's a nag in the back of my head. I'd rather have the nag than the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might wait and see. Is that a plan, or a way of not deciding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both. I'm not a man who changes things before he has to, Lena will tell you that. But with ten years I'd at least know the mortgage and the union are sorted, even if I'm still in the yard every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to do something other than farming at 56, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. Maybe driving, or maintenance at the school with Lena, if they'd have me. I've only ever done cattle, so the honest answer is I'd be starting from nothing.

say: We have **ten years** to make sure the gains are **shared fairly**.
If owners keep all the money, it's **the past** with better kit.
think: Ten years is long enough to **fool myself**, and that's the danger.
At 56 I'd still need **eleven years** of wages before any pension.
do: Wait a year to see whether it's **real** before changing anything at home.
Keep the union pushing for **retraining money** and fair payouts.
Pay the **mortgage down** hard so the house is ours by 2039.
feel: **Calmer**, but with a steady nag at the back of my mind.
S4.quote: If machines do the work and the owners keep the money, that's not the future, that's the past with better kit.
fieldNote: Erik admits his **wait-and-see** habit could be a way of avoiding a decision.
He still expects to lose his job, but at **56**, with the kids grown.
He has **no idea** what other work he'd do, which keeps him anxious.
His politics stay central: **fair sharing** of the gains, not stopping them.

steps.text: Wait a year to see whether the change is real
Keep the union branch pushing for retraining money and payouts
Pay the mortgage down hard so the house is clear by 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years for the office and five for the yard is nothing, and I'd be 48 with a mortgage and two kids still at home. What would help is a law that says if an estate brings in robots, the workers get a year's notice, a proper payout and paid retraining, and a union with the teeth to enforce it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everybody talks about jobs, but nobody asks who notices a cow that's off its feed before it's properly ill. I'd want to know a robot can do that before I'd believe any of this.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about jobs, but nobody asks who notices a cow that's off its feed before it's properly ill.
portrait: Erik Quinn is a **43-year-old head stockman** on a large estate, with a mortgage, a partner and two kids.
He avoids new technology and trusts the **union**, not apps, to protect him.
In the mild pictures his worries are **pay, staffing** and a rising mortgage, not AI.
In the AGI pictures he expects to **lose his job** once robots can do hands-on work.
Longer warning lets him plan for his son and the mortgage, but **not for himself**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, losing his job at 48 with a mortgage and children at home.
whatWouldHelp: A **law on notice** and payouts when estates bring in robots, with paid retraining.
A **union with teeth** to enforce that deal on the estate.
